records.text:
#eyehealth  #healthyvision  #healthyaging  #seniorhealth  
Can the right fruit help support your eyesight as you age? In this 22-minute video, Healing and Health explores the potential benefits of kiwi for eye health and explains how important nutrients such as vitamin C, lutein, and zeaxanthin support healthy vision.

Discover how antioxidants help protect eye cells, why the macula is important for central vision, and how nutrition may contribute to long-term retinal health. We also discuss the role of healthy fats in absorbing certain nutrients, the connection between blood sugar and eye health, and why people over 50 and 60 should pay attention to regular eye examinations.

Learn practical ways to support your vision through a balanced diet, healthy habits, and proactive eye care. Remember, no single fruit can prevent or cure vision loss, but nutrient-rich foods can be part of a healthy lifestyle.

Research and Sources:

National Eye Institute (NEI) — Age-Related Eye Disease Studies (AREDS).

American Journal of Clinical Nutrition — Research on carotenoids and macular pigment.

Journal of Nutrition — Research on avocado and carotenoid absorption.

Diabetes Care — Research on retinal changes associated with prediabetes.

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) — Diabetic Eye Disease and Vision Health.


Subscribe to Healing and Health for evidence-informed videos about eye health, nutrition, healthy aging, and wellness after 50.

Keywords:

 best fruit for eyesight, kiwi benefits for eyes, foods for healthy vision, eye health after 50, eyesight improvement foods, lutein benefits for eyes, zeaxanthin for eye health, vitamin C and eyesight, macular health, retinal health, antioxidants for vision, eye health after 60, nutrition for healthy eyes, prediabetes and eye health, senior eye care

#over60health  #kiwibenefits  #luteina  #zeaxanthin  #MacularHealth #retinalhealth  #visioncare  #eyenutrition  #antioxidants  #prediabetesawareness

 This video is for educational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Consult an eye-care professional for vision concerns and routine eye examinations.

I want to tell you about a single fruit,
one fruit that when you understand what
it does inside your eye, not in your
gut, not in your joints, but
specifically inside your eye, you will
never look at the produce aisle the same
way again. Here is what surprises most
people. It is not the most expensive
fruit. It is not the hardest to find. In
fact, I would be willing to bet that
some of you walk past it every single
week at the grocery store without giving
it a second thought. And yet the
research on what this fruit does to
protect your vision as you age, the
specific mechanism, the way it targets
the exact part of the eye most
vulnerable to damage is some of the most
compelling nutritional science I have
come across in years of studying
preventive medicine. By the end of this
video, you will know exactly which fruit
it is. More importantly, you will know
why, and you will have a simple, honest,
practical way to make it part of your
daily life. starting tomorrow.
I work in preventive health and today we
are talking about your eyes. Stay with
me. But before we get into it, I want to
hear from you. Drop your name and your
age in the comments right now. Tell me
where you are watching from. Are you in
Florida, Ohio, the UK? And tell me this,
when was the last time you genuinely
worried about your eyesight? Because I
think more of you are thinking about
this than you let on. I read every
comment. Let me know you are here. And
if this is your first time on this
channel, welcome. Hit that subscribe
button right now because what we talk
about here is the kind of information
that genuinely changes how you live
every single week. All right, let us get
into it. What is actually happening
inside your aging eye? Let me start with
something that nobody explains clearly
enough. Your eye is not just an organ
that processes light. It is one of the
most metabolically demanding tissues in
your entire body.
The cells in your retina, that paper
thin layer at the back of your eye that
converts light into the signals your
brain reads as vision, those cells burn
energy at an extraordinary rate. They
work around the clock. They never stop.
And here is what that means for you. All
that metabolic activity generates
something called oxidative stress. Think
of it like exhaust from a running
engine. The harder the engine works, the
more exhaust it produces. Your retinal
cells are working constantly, so they
produce a constant stream of free
radicals, unstable molecules that if not
neutralized, begin to damage the very
structures they come from. Now, here is
where it gets specifically important for
anyone over 60. Your body's internal
antioxidant defenses, the systems you
were born with that neutralize those
free radicals, weaken with age. They
simply do not work as efficiently at 65
as they did at 35. This is not a
failure. It is biology. But what it
means practically is that the gap
between the oxidative stress your eyes
generate and your body's ability to
manage it gets wider every decade. And
into that gap, that is where the damage
comes from. Cataracts, macular
degeneration, declining night vision,
increasing sensitivity to glare. These
are not random events. They are the long
slow result of oxidative stress
accumulating in eye tissue that no
longer has the defenses it once did. So
what do most people do about this? Most
people do nothing. Not because they do
not care about their vision, but because
nobody has ever explained the mechanism
to them clearly enough to make it feel
urgent. It feels abstract. It feels like
something that happens to other people.
Until the day your opthalmologist tells
you that your lenses are starting to
cloud. Until the day you reach for a
book and realize the words are blurry in
a way they were not six months ago.
Until the day your grandchild asks why
you are not driving at night anymore and
you do not have a good answer. The point
is this. The eyes you have right now are
the eyes you will have for the rest of
your life. There is no replacement for
them. And the decisions you make about
what you eat, not dramatically, not with
a complicated regimen, but quietly,
consistently, over the years, those
decisions shape the outcome. That is the
foundation. That is why what I am about
to tell you matters. Now, most nutrition
conversations about eye health give you
a list. Five fruits, seven vegetables,
12 supplements. I am not going to do
that today because I think lists without
understanding are forgettable. Instead,
I want to tell you about the one fruit
that researchers keep coming back to.
The one that lines up most precisely
with what your aging eye actually needs.
And the reason it works has everything
to do with where it works. Not in your
bloodstream, not in your stomach,
directly in the macula. If you do not
know what the macula is, stay with me
because this is the whole story. The
macula is a tiny specialized region at
the center of your retina. It is about
the size of a pencil eraser and it is
responsible for virtually everything you
think of as sharp vision. Reading,
recognizing faces, threading a needle,
seeing the numbers on a phone screen,
all of it. That razor sharp central
vision comes from the macula. Here is
what makes the macula extraordinary and
also extraordinarily vulnerable. The
macula contains a unique set of pigments
called macular pigment. These pigments
composed primarily of two compounds
called lutein and zeazanthin function
like a pair of internal sunglasses. They
absorb high energy blue light before it
reaches the most sensitive photo
receptor cells in your eye. They act as
a chemical shield. And here is the
number that should stop you cold.
Studies published in the journal
investigative opthalmology and visual
science have shown that people with
higher macular pigment density have
significantly lower risk of developing
age- related macular degeneration AMD
which is the leading cause of
irreversible vision loss in adults over
50 in the developed world. Not a modest
reduction in risk a significant one. Now
here is the critical piece. Your body
cannot manufacture luteine or zeazanthin
on its own. Not a single molecule. Every
bit of macular pigment you have came
from the food you have eaten across your
lifetime. And as the years go on, if you
are not replenishing it, it thins. Most
Americans are not getting enough. A 2013
National Health and Nutrition
Examination Survey found that the
average American intake of lutein and
zeazanthin is somewhere around 1 to 2
milligs per day. Eye health researchers
generally consider 6 milligs per day of
luteine and 2 milligs of zeazanthin to
be a meaningful protective target.
That is a gap, a quiet, invisible gap
that most people do not know exists
until something goes wrong. So the
question becomes, what fills that gap
most efficiently? What food delivers the
combination of lutein and zeazanthin and
the supporting nutrients the macula
needs in a form the body can actually
absorb that is also realistic for a
regular person to eat regularly? That is
the question the research answers and
the answer is not what most people
expect. Before I tell you the number one
fruit and I am about to I need to tell
you something that most nutrition advice
gets wrong. It is not just about which
nutrients are in a food. It is about
which nutrients your body can actually
get out of it. And this changes
everything about how you evaluate what
you eat for your eyes. The hash shown
fruit and the science behind why. Most
people guess berries and berries are
excellent. I will come back to that.
Some people guess citrus also good. Some
people guess papaya or mango because
they have seen articles about beta
carotene. But the research literature,
when you look at the studies that
specifically measure macular pigment
optical density as an outcome and the
foods that most reliably increase it,
one fruit comes up consistently, kiwi
fruit. Here is why kiwi earns its place
at the top of this list. A study
published in the American Journal of
Clinical Nutrition, a landmark paper
often cited in this field, followed a
group of adults over a 12-week period.
Participants who consume three kiwi
fruits per day showed a meaningful and
measurable increase in macular pigment
optical density. This is not a
theoretical benefit. This is a measured
change in the actual pigment protecting
the center of their retina. Why does
kiwi perform so well? Three reasons.
First, luteine content. Kiwi contains
meaningful amounts of luteine,
approximately 0.1 mg per 100 g.
More relevantly, the luteine and kiwi
appears to be bioavailable, meaning your
body actually absorbs and utilizes it
efficiently. This matters enormously
because luteine from some sources passes
through the body largely unabsorbed.
Second, vitamin C. Ounce for ounce, kiwi
is one of the most vitamin C dense
fruits available. A single kiwi delivers
more vitamin C than an orange of similar
size. And vitamin C is specifically
critical for the lens of your eye. The
lens contains one of the highest
concentrations of vitamin C of any
tissue in the human body and it uses
that vitamin C to defend its proteins
against the oxidative damage that over
decades contributes to cataract
formation. The age related eye disease
study known as ARDS
identified vitamin C as one of the key
nutrients associated with reduced risk
of cataract progression. Third, vitamin
E. Kiwi contains vitamin E which
protects the membranes of your photo
receptor cells, the rods and cones that
actually convert light into signals.
Vitamin E is fat soluble which means it
works within the fatty membranes of
these cells in a way water- soluble
vitamins cannot. So in one small fruit
smaller than your fist, you have lutein
for the macula, vitamin C for the lens

Three layers of protection, three
different parts of the eye addressed

These are exactly the outcomes that

While the pigment is still there to

a handful of blueberries several

working age adults in the United States.
But here is what many people do not

early microvascular changes in the

of diabetic retinopathy. The small blood

flag this honestly. If you have diabetes

how to incorporate fruit into your
specific dietary pattern is worth
having. Blood sugar management is not
separate from my health. It is central
to it. And the daily choices you make
about what you eat, how much you move,

are among the most powerful things you

downstream of everything else in your

pressure is poorly controlled, the eye

If you want to be the first to see it

Take care of yourself. Take care of your
